[Jonesboro, GA](https://maps.app.goo.gl/j295z6UNFrveGDVz9) [(770) 603-8511](tel:\(770\) 603-8511) [Text Us](sms:\(404\) 383-8194)

 

# How Much to Charge for Mobile Dog Grooming: A Pricing Method

November 7th, 2026 | By A&A Center Trailers

![New mobile pet grooming trailer at A&A Center Trailers in Jonesboro, GA](/edge-assets/blog/how-much-to-charge-for-mobile-dog-grooming-1000w-add07c3e.webp)

One of the first questions every new mobile groomer asks is how much to charge. Copying the salon down the street is tempting, but a mobile business has different costs and offers clients something a salon cannot: you come to them. Your prices should reflect both.

Instead of guessing, use a method. Work out what each groom actually costs you, add what you need to earn, and then check the result against your local market.

## Step 1: Add Up Your Fixed Monthly Costs

These are the costs you pay whether you groom 10 dogs or 100:

*   Your trailer payment, if you financed it
*   Your tow vehicle payment
*   Insurance on the trailer, the vehicle, your business liability and the animals in your care
*   Phone, booking software and website
*   Business license and professional fees
*   Marketing
*   Money set aside for maintenance and equipment replacement

## Step 2: Estimate Your Variable Costs Per Groom

These go up with every appointment:

*   Shampoo, conditioner and other products
*   Blades, sharpening and small tools
*   Towels, laundry and sanitation supplies
*   Water
*   Generator fuel
*   Fuel for driving between appointments

Track these for a few weeks once you start. Your real numbers will beat any estimate.

## Step 3: Be Honest About Capacity

Mobile groomers usually do fewer dogs per day than a busy salon because of drive time, setup and one-on-one handling. That is fine. It is part of what clients pay for. Figure out how many grooms you can realistically do per day, then multiply by the days you will work each month. Leave room for cancellations, rain days and slow seasons.

## Step 4: Find Your Cost Per Groom

Use this formula:

Cost per groom = (fixed monthly costs ÷ grooms per month) + variable cost per groom

That number is your break-even. Charge less and you lose money on every dog, even if the calendar is full.

## Step 5: Add Your Pay and Profit

Your break-even does not include your own wages. Decide what you need to earn per month, divide it by your grooms per month, and add it. Then add a profit margin for growth, slow months and the next trailer.

| Line | How to calculate |
| --- | --- |
| Fixed cost per groom | Fixed monthly costs ÷ grooms per month |
| Variable cost per groom | Supplies, water, generator fuel and road fuel per appointment |
| Your pay per groom | Monthly income goal ÷ grooms per month |
| Profit | A percentage of the subtotal for growth and reserves |
| Base price | The total of the four lines above |

## Step 6: Build a Price List

A single base price is a starting point. Real dogs vary, so most groomers price by:

*   Size: small, medium, large and giant breeds take different time and product.
*   Coat type: double coats, doodles and heavy undercoats take longer.
*   Service: full groom, bath and tidy, nails only.
*   Condition: a matted coat or a dog who needs extra handling takes more time.

Base each tier on the time it really takes. If a doodle takes twice as long as a small terrier, it should cost noticeably more.

### Add-Ons

Teeth brushing, special shampoos, nail grinding and de-shedding treatments add value for clients and income for you.

### Travel Zones

Some groomers include travel within a core service area and add a fee for appointments farther out. Zones also help you group appointments by neighborhood, which cuts drive time.

## Step 7: Check Your Local Market

Now compare your numbers with what salons and other mobile groomers in your area charge. Call a few, check their websites and read their reviews. If your price lands far above the market, look for ways to cut drive time or raise capacity. If it lands well below, you may be underpricing the convenience you offer.

Groomer communities like the [AKC Groomer Hub](https://www.akc.org/groomer-hub/) are a good place to learn how other groomers handle pricing, policies and client communication.

## Policies That Protect Your Prices

Your pricing only works if your calendar holds. Put a few simple policies in writing and share them when clients book:

*   Cancellations and no-shows: how much notice you need, and what happens without it.
*   Matted coats: when a dematting fee applies, or when a shave-down is the humane choice.
*   Behavior: how you handle a dog that needs extra time or handling.
*   Payment: how and when you collect.

## Raising Your Prices

Costs rise, and your prices should follow. Give existing clients notice before a change, explain it briefly and keep the message friendly. Clients who value a groomer who comes to their door and knows their dog usually understand. New clients can start at your new rates right away.

## Is Mobile Grooming Profitable?

It can be, when your prices cover your real costs and your schedule stays full. Routes matter: grouping appointments by area cuts fuel and lets you fit more grooms into the day. Repeat clients on a regular schedule smooth out your income. Review your prices at least once a year as costs change.

## Your Trailer Is Part of the Math

Your grooming trailer is one of your largest fixed costs, so it is worth getting right. Our built-to-order grooming trailers start at $13,100, and our [dog grooming trailer cost guide](https://www.aacenter.net/dog-grooming-trailer-cost) explains what each tier includes. If you are still deciding between platforms, read our comparison of a [pet grooming van vs. trailer](https://www.aacenter.net/blog/pet-grooming-van-vs-trailer), or design a [custom mobile grooming trailer](https://www.aacenter.net/dog-grooming-trailer) around your workflow.

Come walk through a grooming trailer at 8834 Tara Blvd, Jonesboro, GA 30236, just south of Atlanta. We are open Monday to Friday 9 AM to 5 PM and Saturday 9 AM to 4 PM. Call [(770) 603-8511](tel:+17706038511) or text [(404) 383-8194](sms:+14043838194) and tell us how you want your grooming day to run.

# What is the Cost to Start a Mobile Dog Grooming Business vs. a Franchise?

July 1, 2026

Share Share

 Link

Close share Copy link

The pet industry continues to experience explosive growth, and entrepreneurs entering the market in 2026 have more opportunities than ever before. But for many aspiring business owners, one major question comes up early in the decision-making process: Should you start your own mobile grooming business or invest in a pet grooming franchise?

Both paths can lead to success. Both offer access to a growing market of pet owners willing to invest in professional care. However, the differences in startup costs, flexibility, profit potential, and long-term control can significantly impact your future. If you are considering entering the pet grooming industry, **understanding the pros and cons of each model is essential before making an investment**. Let's break it down.

## The Appeal of Pet Franchises

Franchises have long been marketed as a safer route into entrepreneurship. Instead of building a business from scratch, franchise owners gain access to an established brand, proven operating systems, training programs, and marketing support. For first-time entrepreneurs, this structure can feel reassuring. In many cases, franchises provide:

*   Brand recognition
*   Operational guidelines
*   Marketing materials
*   Initial training
*   Ongoing support

Because the framework already exists, owners do not have to spend as much time developing processes or creating a brand identity from the ground up. For some people, this level of support is exactly what they are looking for. But convenience often comes with trade-offs.

![](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0587/4191/5702/files/27_-_1.png?v=1783010792)

## The Hidden Costs of Franchise Ownership

One of the biggest misconceptions about franchises is that they simplify business ownership without significantly affecting profitability. In reality, **franchise ownership often includes a variety of ongoing costs that can reduce long-term earnings**. Depending on the franchise, owners may be responsible for:

*   Initial franchise fees
*   Royalty payments
*   Marketing fees
*   Technology fees
*   Renewal costs

These expenses continue regardless of how successful the business becomes. As revenue grows, so do many of these fees. While franchise systems provide support, entrepreneurs should carefully evaluate whether the ongoing costs align with their financial goals. After all, the more revenue you generate, the more you will likely pay back to the franchise organization.

## What Is The Cost to Start a Mobile Dog Grooming Business?

Over the past several years, mobile grooming has emerged as one of the fastest-growing segments of the pet industry. Consumers increasingly value convenience, personalized service, and premium experiences. Mobile grooming delivers all three. Instead of requiring pet owners to drive to a salon, wait for appointments, and manage transportation logistics, groomers bring the service directly to the client's doorstep.

This convenience creates strong customer demand while allowing business owners to operate with greater flexibility. Perhaps most importantly, **mobile grooming gives entrepreneurs complete ownership of their business**. There are no royalty payments. No franchise restrictions. No corporate approvals required for every decision. You control your pricing, marketing, service offerings, and future.

## Freedom and Flexibility Matter

For many entrepreneurs, flexibility is one of the strongest advantages of independent ownership. Franchise systems typically require adherence to specific operating procedures, branding guidelines, and service structures. While these rules create consistency, they can also limit creativity and innovation. **Independent mobile grooming businesses have the freedom to evolve** in response to customer demand.

*   Want to introduce premium spa treatments?
*   Adjust your service area?
*   Create unique membership programs?
*   Offer luxury add-ons?

As an independent owner, those decisions are entirely yours. This flexibility becomes particularly valuable as consumer preferences continue to evolve in 2026 and beyond.

![](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0587/4191/5702/files/27_-_2.png?v=1783010813)

## Startup Costs: Comparing the Investment

At first glance, the investment required can seem substantial, but when you discover the real mobile dog grooming business profit potential, it is totally worth it. You will need a reliable van, a professional conversion, insurance, equipment, branding, and marketing. However, franchise opportunities often require similar investments — plus franchise fees and recurring royalty obligations.

The difference is where your money goes. **With mobile grooming, your investment primarily builds equity in assets you own**, such as your vehicle, equipment, and brand. With a franchise, a portion of your investment supports access to someone else's system. For entrepreneurs focused on long-term wealth building, ownership can be a compelling advantage.

## Building a Brand That Belongs to You

One of the most rewarding aspects of entrepreneurship is creating something that reflects your vision. When you build an independent mobile grooming business, every success contributes to your brand's value.

*   Your reputation
*   Your customer relationships
*   Your online reviews
*   Your growth

Everything belongs to you. Over time, this can become a significant asset. Rather than promoting a franchise brand

### [What Animal Care and Service Workers Do](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#tab-2)

Animal care and service workers attend to or train animals.

### [Work Environment](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#tab-3)

Animal care and service workers are employed in a variety of settings, including kennels, zoos, stables, animal shelters, pet stores, veterinary clinics, and aquariums. Some parts of the job may be physically or emotionally demanding, and workers risk injury when caring for animals.

### [How to Become an Animal Care and Service Worker](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#tab-4)

Animal care and service workers typically have a high school diploma or equivalent and learn the occupation on the job. Many employers prefer to hire candidates who have experience working with animals.

### [Pay](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#tab-5)

The median annual wage for animal caretakers was $35,360 in May 2025.

The median annual wage for animal trainers was $39,990 in May 2025.

### [Job Outlook](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#tab-6)

Overall employment of animal care and service workers is projected to grow 11 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations.

About 69,400 openings for animal care and service workers are projected each year, on average, over the decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire.

## What Animal Care and Service Workers Do[About this section](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/animal-care-and-service-workers.htm#TB_inline?height=325&width=325&inlineId=about-what-they-do)

Animal care and service workers attend to or train animals. Working with pets and other nonfarm animals, these caretakers and trainers feed, groom, and exercise the animals or teach them to respond to human commands.

### Duties

Animal care and service workers typically do the following:

*   Give food and water to animals
*   Clean equipment and the living spaces of animals
*   Monitor animals and record details of their diet, physical condition, and behavior
*   Examine animals for signs of illness or injury
*   Exercise animals
*   Bathe animals, trim nails, clip hair, and attend to other grooming needs
*   Train animals to obey or to behave in a specific manner

The following are types of animal care and service workers:

**_Animal trainers_** teach animals a variety of skills, such as obedience, performance, riding, security, and assisting people with disabilities. They familiarize animals with human voices and contact, and they teach animals to respond to commands. Most animal trainers work with dogs and horses, but some work with marine mammals, such as dolphins. Trainers teach a variety of skills.
